evidence.title: Venice: departure with father and uncle
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: The prologue places Marco with Niccolò and Maffeo on the departure for Acre.
evidence.limits: Marco did not accompany their earlier Asian journey. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Acre: papal negotiations
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: The account brings the three Polos to Acre during preparations for travel east.
evidence.limits: The family’s movements around Acre include return visits; the point is not an exact dated arrival. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Ayas: Cilician gateway
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: Ayas, called Laiazzo, appears in the departure sequence between Acre and inland Asia.
evidence.limits: The map simplifies repeated journeys between these ports. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Mainland Hormuz: outward-journey reconstruction
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: Polo describes Curmos as a port receiving Indian merchandise.
evidence.limits: This is an approximate mainland old-Hormuz anchor near Minab, not the later island city. The book supplies no secure stop year. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Kashgar: described in the eastward sequence
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: The Cascar chapter describes an oasis of gardens, crafts and merchants.
evidence.limits: A place in the book’s geographical sequence is not an independently dated personal visit. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Shangdu: reported arrival at Kublai’s court
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: Shangdu is conventionally identified with the court reached near the end of the outward journey.
evidence.limits: The arrival year is a historical reconstruction; palace descriptions do not locate every movement of the Polos. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Khanbaliq: the court described in the book
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: The account describes Kublai’s winter court at Cambaluc, present-day Beijing.
evidence.limits: This broad narrative setting does not imply uninterrupted residence or confirm every claimed office. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Hangzhou: a detailed city description
evidence.dateLabel: After the 1276 conquest, within the reported Yuan years
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: Quinsai is identified as Hangzhou, whose waterways, markets and urban life receive extended treatment.
evidence.limits: No precise visit year is established here. Manuscript versions differ; the book’s impressive numbers are not used as a census. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Quanzhou: reported embarkation for the return
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: The return is conventionally reconstructed as embarking at Quanzhou, the book’s Çaiton.
evidence.limits: The departure date is approximate. Independent port archaeology establishes the trading setting, not Polo’s individual presence. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Northern Sumatra: a claimed weather delay
evidence.dateLabel: Within the return voyage, about 1292–1293 CE
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: In the Samarra chapter, Marco explicitly claims a five-month stay caused by bad weather.
evidence.limits: The kingdom’s exact identification and the travel chronology remain uncertain; this point represents northern Sumatra broadly. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Mainland Hormuz: reported sea-journey endpoint
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: The maritime return is reconstructed as reaching Hormuz before travel back toward the Mediterranean.
evidence.limits: The broad date is not a harbor log; old mainland Hormuz is represented approximately. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Trebizond: named on the homeward route
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: The prologue names Trebizond among the stages of the return west.
evidence.limits: The text gives a sequence, not an exact arrival date. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Constantinople: named on the homeward route
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: Constantinople follows Trebizond in the prologue’s homeward sequence.
evidence.limits: This date window is inferred from the return narrative, not proof of continuous residence. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Negroponte: a homeward stop
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: The prologue lists Negroponte, the Venetian name associated with Euboea, before Venice.
evidence.limits: Chalkis is a regional harbor anchor; the text does not supply an exact landing location or day. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Venice: the stated return
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: The prologue dates the family’s arrival back in Venice to 1295.
evidence.limits: Arrival is a biographical event, not a foundation or population estimate for Venice. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Genoa: a book takes shape
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar CE; broad interval of the reported journey, not independently dated presence or the settlement’s lifespan.
evidence.summary: Tradition places the production of Polo’s account with Rustichello during imprisonment in Genoa.
evidence.limits: This marks the account’s composition context, not another stop on the Asian journey; circumstances of capture remain debated. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Japan / Cipangu: described, not visited
evidence.dateBasis: Approximate composition date of the surviving narrative tradition, not an occupation or visit date.
evidence.summary: The book’s Cipangu material belongs to secondhand reporting about Japan.
evidence.limits: No Polo journey connection leads here. The date marks the account, and the regional anchor does not identify a landing or settlement. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Chang’an: foundation of Weiyang Palace
evidence.dateBasis: Institutional chronology gives 200 BCE; astronomical year = 1 − 200 = −199.
evidence.summary: Weiyang Palace places a major Han political center at the eastern end of later exchange corridors.
evidence.limits: A palace-construction date is not the birth date of an entire transcontinental network. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Taxila: the foundation of Sirkap
evidence.dateBasis: Approximate founding anchor: 150 BCE maps to astronomical −149; original source says mid-second century BCE.
evidence.summary: The fortified Sirkap settlement illustrates urban development at a South Asian crossroads.
evidence.limits: 150 BCE is a display anchor for 'mid-second century BCE', not an exact founding year. The wider Taxila landscape is much older. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Luoyang: Eastern Han capital
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar dates of the selected archaeological or architectural phase; century boundaries are display conventions, not exact construction or abandonment years.
evidence.summary: Luoyang anchors an imperial urban phase at the eastern end of the corridor system.
evidence.limits: The interval selects one capital phase; it is not the complete lifespan of Luoyang. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Palmyra: caravan oasis and monumental city
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar dates of the selected archaeological or architectural phase; century boundaries are display conventions, not exact construction or abandonment years.
evidence.summary: The surviving urban ensemble reflects connections between local, Mediterranean and Persian traditions.
evidence.limits: Architectural influence is not proof that every resident or object travelled the whole distance to China. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Berenike: a Red Sea trading port
evidence.dateLabel: Periplus context: mid-to-late first century CE
evidence.dateBasis: The account is usually placed in the mid-first century CE; 50–100 is a deliberately broad display interval.
evidence.summary: The Periplus begins its maritime geography with Egyptian Red Sea ports including Berenike.
evidence.limits: This is a broad textual activity window, not the foundation date of the port. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Cana: Arabian incense and sea connections
evidence.dateLabel: Periplus context: mid-to-late first century CE
evidence.dateBasis: Broad first-century CE textual activity window; not settlement founding or abandonment.
evidence.summary: The Periplus describes Cana receiving incense from inland and trading with Indian and Persian ports.
evidence.limits: Bir Ali is an approximate locality identification; the narrative does not establish a timeless shipping lane. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Barygaza: navigation and local expertise
evidence.dateLabel: Periplus context: mid-to-late first century CE
evidence.dateBasis: Broad first-century CE textual activity window; not settlement founding or abandonment.
evidence.summary: The account describes river pilots helping ships negotiate the approach to Barygaza, near modern Bharuch.
evidence.limits: The source describes particular commercial conditions; it is not a census or a complete port history. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Niya: documents from an oasis society
evidence.dateBasis: University catalogue’s approximate date range for the Kharosthi documents.
evidence.summary: Kharosthi documents preserve administration and everyday transactions in the Niya oasis region.
evidence.limits: Dates describe the document corpus; its people and institutions cannot be reduced to passing caravans. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Near Dunhuang: the Sogdian Ancient Letters
evidence.dateBasis: Scholarly dating of the letters to 313/314 CE, not their 1907 discovery.
evidence.summary: Letters recovered west of Dunhuang connect merchant households, distant business and interrupted communications.
evidence.limits: The findspot is represented near the western frontier corridor, not the town center. Dating is a scholarly reconstruction. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Mogao: a long sequence of Buddhist caves
evidence.dateLabel: From 366 CE; principal sequence through the fourteenth century
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar dates of the selected archaeological or architectural phase; century boundaries are display conventions, not exact construction or abandonment years.
evidence.summary: Cave temples and manuscripts document many centuries of religious and artistic activity near Dunhuang.
evidence.limits: The endpoint rounds the end of the fourteenth century; individual caves have different dates and later histories. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Ancient Penjikent: an inhabited Sogdian town
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar dates of the selected archaeological or architectural phase; century boundaries are display conventions, not exact construction or abandonment years.
evidence.summary: Excavation reveals houses, temples, workshops and monumental art in an urban settlement.
evidence.limits: The broad archaeological interval is not an exact foundation-to-destruction chronology. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Suyab: a changing urban and religious center
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar dates of the selected archaeological or architectural phase; century boundaries are display conventions, not exact construction or abandonment years.
evidence.summary: Archaeology at Ak-Beshim documents a city with Buddhist, Christian and other religious material.
evidence.limits: The broad period includes rebuilding and political change; cultural labels do not identify a uniform population. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Balasagun: a Chuy valley city
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar dates of the selected archaeological or architectural phase; century boundaries are display conventions, not exact construction or abandonment years.
evidence.summary: Burana represents the medieval city of Balasagun and its surviving religious architecture.
evidence.limits: A broad occupation interval does not imply unchanged boundaries, rulers or population. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Bukhara: Samanid architectural evidence
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar dates of the selected archaeological or architectural phase; century boundaries are display conventions, not exact construction or abandonment years.
evidence.summary: The Samanid mausoleum anchors an early medieval architectural phase in Bukhara.
evidence.limits: The city predates this monument; much visible urban fabric belongs to later periods. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Merv: Seljuk capital phase
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar dates of the selected archaeological or architectural phase; century boundaries are display conventions, not exact construction or abandonment years.
evidence.summary: Merv’s archaeological landscape includes a major Seljuk capital phase.
evidence.limits: This selected phase is only part of a much longer sequence of settlements in the oasis. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Quanzhou: a Song–Yuan maritime emporium
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar dates of the selected archaeological or architectural phase; century boundaries are display conventions, not exact construction or abandonment years.
evidence.summary: Ports, bridges, religious monuments and production sites document an extensive trading city and its hinterland.
evidence.limits: The component sites have different histories; the interval describes the emporium phase, not simultaneous construction. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Tana: a merchant handbook’s western starting point
evidence.dateBasis: Circa 1340 CE is a composition/display anchor, not a foundation or visit date.
evidence.summary: Pegolotti’s instructions start the overland journey to Cathay at Tana, near modern Azov.
evidence.limits: The approximate date belongs to the handbook; Pegolotti did not claim to have personally travelled this entire route. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Urgench: a trading stop in Pegolotti
evidence.dateBasis: Circa 1340 CE is a composition/display anchor, not a foundation or visit date.
evidence.summary: The handbook recommends Urgench as a place where merchants could sell goods on the journey east.
evidence.limits: This is advice about a route, not a dated expedition or a measurement of traffic. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

evidence.title: Samarkand: Timurid urban development
evidence.dateBasis: Calendar dates of the selected archaeological or architectural phase; century boundaries are display conventions, not exact construction or abandonment years.
evidence.summary: The Timurid city’s monuments and plan represent a later phase of Central Asian urban connections.
evidence.limits: Samarkand’s older Afrasiab settlement has a separate history; this date range does not imply uninterrupted prosperity. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors.

waves.title: Reported departure: Venice, Acre and Ayas
waves.summary: A schematic opening phase of the family’s eastward journey.
waves.limits: The actual sequence included repeated movements between Acre and Ayas, simplified here. Lines connect broad regions; bends are illustrative and do not locate camps, tracks or population volumes.

waves.title: Reconstructed outward journey across Asia
waves.summary: The broad reconstruction connects the Iranian detour, Central Asian oasis sequence and reported arrival at Kublai’s court.
waves.limits: Many intermediate dates and identifications are uncertain. This is a synthesis of the narrative, not a recovered itinerary; described places do not all establish visits. Lines connect broad regions; bends are illustrative and do not locate camps, tracks or population volumes.

waves.title: Reported return by the Indian Ocean
waves.summary: The return reconstruction joins Quanzhou, northern Sumatra and Hormuz through the Indian Ocean.
waves.limits: The route is schematic, including broad sea bends around South and Southeast Asia. Stop dates, vessel tracks and several place identifications remain uncertain. Lines connect broad regions; bends are illustrative and do not locate camps, tracks or population volumes.

waves.title: Return through the Black Sea and Mediterranean
waves.summary: The homeward sequence ends in Venice in 1295.
waves.limits: Trebizond, Constantinople and Negroponte are named in the prologue; the connecting geometry and intermediate dates are reconstructed. Lines connect broad regions; bends are illustrative and do not locate camps, tracks or population volumes.

waves.title: Formative eastern overland corridors
waves.summary: A selected eastern corridor phase links Han political centers, the Hexi corridor and oasis routes.
waves.limits: UNESCO dates the corridor’s formation broadly. This is a network example; it does not date one continuous road or a single end-to-end caravan. Lines connect broad regions; bends are illustrative and do not locate camps, tracks or population volumes.

waves.title: Red Sea, Arabia and western India
waves.summary: The Periplus documents overlapping maritime markets and sailing knowledge.
waves.limits: A broad first-century scene combines connections described in the text; it is not the itinerary of one ship or a year-round lane. Lines connect broad regions; bends are illustrative and do not locate camps, tracks or population volumes.

waves.title: Sogdian letters: long-distance commercial ties
waves.summary: The letters link business and households in China with a Samarkand-centered commercial world.
waves.limits: This is a relationship between documented regions, not a reconstructed postal path. Disrupted communications are part of the evidence. Lines connect broad regions; bends are illustrative and do not locate camps, tracks or population volumes.

waves.title: Zarafshan–Karakum exchange corridor
waves.summary: A medieval phase joins the Zarafshan cities, Bukhara and Merv within the documented corridor.
waves.limits: The range follows a broad phase identified by UNESCO; activity was uneven and the links were part of a larger network. Lines connect broad regions; bends are illustrative and do not locate camps, tracks or population volumes.

waves.title: Pegolotti’s western caravan stages
waves.summary: The handbook connects Tana with Volga and Central Asian trading stages toward Urgench.
waves.limits: These are commercial instructions, not Pegolotti’s own expedition. Sarai’s precise localization and the route geometry are simplified. Lines connect broad regions; bends are illustrative and do not locate camps, tracks or population volumes.

waves.title: Pegolotti’s onward connection toward Cathay
waves.summary: The handbook’s onward sequence reaches Chinese markets, including Qinsai (Hangzhou), before the capital at Khanbaliq.
waves.limits: Medieval place-name identifications and alternative branches are uncertain; the line compresses them into a legible connection. Lines connect broad regions; bends are illustrative and do not locate camps, tracks or population volumes.

studies.title: Marco Polo: journey and account
studies.summary: Follow the reported journeys, the cities described and the uncertainties of a thirteenth-century account.

studies.title: Silk Roads: cities and connections
studies.summary: Explore selected land and sea networks through dated settlements, letters, monuments and trading instructions.
